questions.q: Why are frozen base weights a comparatively safe target for aggressive 4-bit quantization in QLoRA?
options: Because frozen weights are never actually read during training
Because they never receive gradient updates, so a one-time precision loss from quantization is a static accuracy cost rather than a training-stability problem
Because 4-bit quantization has zero effect on accuracy
Because frozen weights are always smaller than LoRA adapters
questions.explain: Since frozen weights only need to be read during the forward pass and never updated, quantizing them to 4-bit is a one-time accuracy trade-off rather than a risk to training stability, unlike quantizing actively-trained weights.

questions.q: What distinguishes NF4 (NormalFloat4) from a naive, evenly-spaced 4-bit integer format?
options: NF4 uses 8 bits instead of 4
NF4 allocates more representable values near zero, matching the approximately normal distribution of real pretrained weights, minimizing quantization error for actual weight statistics
NF4 only works for embedding layers
NF4 is identical to a standard integer format but renamed
questions.explain: NF4 is designed around the empirical observation that pretrained weights are roughly normally distributed, so it places more representable values near zero rather than spacing them evenly, reducing quantization error.

questions.q: What does "double quantization" refer to in QLoRA?
options: Quantizing the model weights twice to 4-bit for extra compression
Quantizing the per-block scaling constants used to dequantize the 4-bit weights, squeezing out additional memory savings with negligible extra accuracy loss
Running the forward pass twice for better accuracy
Training two separate LoRA adapters simultaneously
questions.explain: Double quantization applies quantization to the quantization constants themselves (the per-block scaling factors), saving additional memory with minimal accuracy impact.

questions.q: What does `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16` control in a QLoRA setup?
options: The precision used to store the frozen weights on disk permanently
The precision used for on-the-fly dequantized matrix multiplication during the actual forward/backward computation, even though weights are stored in 4-bit
The precision of the tokenizer's vocabulary
Whether double quantization is enabled
questions.explain: While the base weights are stored in 4-bit (NF4), they are dequantized on the fly for the actual matrix multiplications, and compute_dtype specifies that dequantized compute happens in bfloat16.

questions.q: What practical capability did QLoRA's paper demonstrate that was not achievable with full-precision LoRA alone?
options: Training a model with zero GPUs
Fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU, since even the frozen bf16 weights of a model that large wouldn't otherwise fit
Eliminating the need for any training data
Running inference without any GPU at all
questions.explain: QLoRA's headline result showed a 65B-parameter model could be fine-tuned on a single 48GB GPU, which full-precision LoRA could not achieve since the frozen bf16 weights alone would exceed that GPU's memory.
